original_value: AbstractIn this study, geographic information system (GIS)‐based network analysis and analytic hierarchy process (AHP) methods were applied to the Erzincan–Trabzon segment of the Turkish high‐speed railway (HSR) project. A new hybrid route, which considers both economic and environmental criteria, was created and compared with three different routes from various preconstruction studies. The route‐generating analysis included the eight parameters (criteria) of slope, geology, soil quality, rivers, protected areas, roads, land cover, and lakes. The optimum route for connecting the port of Trabzon to Turkey's interior via HSR was generated. The weights for determining the route were tested for sensitivity. The study demonstrated the efficiency of GIS and AHP integration in generating optimum routes for HSR projects according to given databases. All these GIS and AHP analyses were applied automatically with our novel GIS extension for determining optimum HSR routes. The final route has preserved cultural and historical structures, environmental integrity. The new hybrid route also decreased construction costs by approximately 12%, and the least‐cost‐path analysis confirmed the environmental efficiency of the route.

result.paraphrase: Abstract: This study applied GIS-based network analysis and the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) to the Erzincan–Trabzon section of the Turkish high-speed railway (HSR) project. A new hybrid route was designed with both economic and environmental criteria in mind and compared with three routes from prior preconstruction studies. The route-generation analysis used eight criteria: slope, geology, soil quality, rivers, protected areas, roads, land cover, and lakes. It produced the optimum HSR route for linking Trabzon port to Turkey’s interior. Route-determination weights were subjected to sensitivity testing. The study showed that integrating GIS and AHP is effective for producing optimum HSR routes from the available databases. All GIS and AHP analyses were carried out automatically using our novel GIS extension for determining optimum HSR routes. The final route preserved cultural and historical structures as well as environmental integrity. The new hybrid route also reduced construction costs by about 12%, and least-cost-path analysis confirmed its environmental efficiency.
